questions.question: React.memo vs useMemo vs useCallback — which does what?
questions.title: React.memo vs useMemo vs useCallback — Differences & Use Cases
questions.direct_answer:
React.memo vs useMemo vs useCallback — which does what?

**In one line:** name the mechanism, where it applies (the framework runtime (render, reconciliation, DI, CD) and the browser), and the user-visible outcome.

**Interviewers dig into:** React.memo wraps a component (props equality); useMemo caches a value; useCallback caches a function; all use dep arrays.

**Classic weak answer:** Adding React.memo to every component — without stable props, memo does nothing except add comparison overhead.

**Senior finish:** Mention React Compiler (2024) auto-memoizes; default rule: don't memoize until profiler shows benefit.

sections.title: Why this question matters
sections.content:
This question — **React.memo vs useMemo vs useCallback — Differences & Use Cases** — shows up constantly in **frontend / fullstack** interviews because it separates candidates who memorized docs from candidates who can **reason about real systems**.

**Restate the prompt:** React.memo vs useMemo vs useCallback — which does what?

A gold-level answer does four things in order:

1. **Define** the terms in plain English (what it is / what problem it solves).
2. **Explain the mechanism** (what runs when: browser, bundler, framework, network).
3. **Compare trade-offs** (speed vs correctness vs security vs DX) with **when you would not use** the default.
4. **Ground it in production** — caching, auth, observability, tests, or an incident you handled.

Interviewers are listening for: **React.memo wraps a component (props equality); useMemo caches a value; useCallback caches a function; all use dep arrays**.

The fastest way to lose points is: **Adding React.memo to every component — without stable props, memo does nothing except add comparison overhead**.

If you only add one “senior” layer, make it: **Mention React Compiler (2024) auto-memoizes; default rule: don't memoize until profiler shows benefit**.

sections.title: Deep dive — what to say
sections.content:
### What to explain (middle of the answer)

- **Core mechanics:** React.memo wraps a component (props equality); useMemo caches a value; useCallback caches a function; all use dep arrays
- **Concrete shape:** give a small code or config snippet *only if it clarifies* (5–15 lines max).
- **Interviewer follow-ups:** expect “what breaks in production?”, “how do you debug?”, “what would you measure?” — answer them proactively.

### How to sound senior (without rambling)

- Tie the feature to **user-visible outcomes** (performance, accessibility, security).
- Mention **one failure mode** you have actually seen (race, stale cache, hydration mismatch, flaky test).
- Close with **one decision rule** (“choose X when …; choose Y when …”).

sections.content:

- **DX vs constraints** (framework magic vs explicit wiring).
- **SEO / first paint vs interactivity** (SSR/SSG/CSR choices where relevant).
- **Security vs convenience** (tokens, cookies, localStorage, third-party scripts).

### What “book answer” misses

- **Book answer:** repeats definitions.
- **Strong answer:** names **adding React.memo to every component — without stable props, memo does nothing except add comparison overhead** and what you do instead.

questions.question: When can memoization actually HURT React performance?
questions.title: When Memoization Hurts React Performance — Common Bugs
questions.direct_answer:
When can memoization actually HURT React performance?

**In one line:** name the mechanism, where it applies (the framework runtime (render, reconciliation, DI, CD) and the browser), and the user-visible outcome.

**Interviewers dig into:** Dep comparison cost, stale values, memory overhead, deep-equal checks, unstable deps that change every render.

**Classic weak answer:** Deep-equaling objects in React.memo's equality function — the check can cost more than the render.

**Senior finish:** Share profiler workflows (React DevTools Profiler, Chrome Performance), and stress 'measure first'.
